newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-German economic recovery on track - Issing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German economic recovery on track - Issing.

text.p: The stage is set for Germany's economic recovery to continue and gather pace, Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said on Friday.
In a speech to Swiss bankers, he added that an interest rate cut now would be counterproductive and would not help put the unemployed back to work.

Issing said he saw no signs of exchange rate tension in Europe in the light of the dollar's strength and told Reuters Financial Television he expected Europe's single currency project to start on time in 1999.
"As far as foreign exchange rates, the price situation and unit wage costs go, everything is in place for the upturn to continue and strengthen," Issing said.
"We can expect this, although there are still some areas of uncertainty on hand."
He dismissed calls for Germany's central bank to cut interest rates as a way to help put 4.5 million unemployed Germans back to work.
"Interest rate cuts would be absolutely counterproductive. If we (the Bundesbank) were to lower (rates), capital market rates would move in the other direction," Issing said.
Asked about the effects of the dollar's recent rise against the mark, he declined to comment directly.
But he said: "In Europe...there are no signs of exchange rate tensions," adding that one should not focus too much on short-term or daily fluctuations.
He attributed the recent rise in sterling to the British government's decision to give the Bank of England freedom to set interest rates, providing more protection from short-term political pressure.
Issing said inflation remained under control in Germany, commenting: "We are in quiet waters as far as prices are concerned."

The one area to watch was import prices, where higher energy prices denominated in dollars and the weak mark had potential to fuel inflation but this was being compensated by declining unit-wage costs.
He reiterated calls for a narrow and strict interpretation of Maastricht Treaty criteria that are supposed to determine which countries qualify to launch the single euro currency in 1999.

He added that plans for Europe's single currency were adding to uncertainty in the current outlook and it would be advantageous to determine the conversion of individual currencies into the euro at the earliest possible time.
Issing said a timely start to the third phase of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) on January 1, 1999 was still the most likely scenario.

Asked whether Germany's budget problems could lead to a delay to the start a single European currency, Issing said: "I would not say that it is mainly Germany that causes such deliberations over delay. I think EMU will start on time. This is still the most probable (case)."

He added that not only Germany but also other countries had a lot of work to do to live up to a strict and narrow interpretation of the Maastricht economic convergence criteria, as the German parliament has demanded.
He refused to be drawn on whether he thought Germany could get its 1997 budget deficit down to three percent of gross domestic product, as the treaty requires.

"The deficit criterion of three percent is endangered, therefore Finance Minister (Theo) Waigel has announced he will present a supplementary budget next week to the government. We have to wait and see what is done to come closer to this three percent criterion," he said.
Asked if optimism about this was in order, he said: "I don't know. It is a very (difficult) task for him, so we just have to wait and see."
The German economy's performance was "not bad" in April and May but special factors made comparisons difficult, he said.
First-quarter gross domestic product growth came in slightly better than expected at 0.5 percent versus the previous quarter.

"The data we have seen since then confirm this impression. Based on the information we have, April and May were not so bad," he said, but the fact that Easter fell in March this year and May had so many holidays made the data hard to assess.

"I mention this not because it is so important but because order inflow data for May and production numbers have just been published. They do not appear intoxicating but they have to be seen against this background."
German industrial orders fell 0.8 percent in May compared with April, breaking a four-month uptrend. Industrial output edged down 0.2 percent in May from April, its first fall since January.
